The challenge: a writer with everything but a website

Lilitu Rodac had the hard parts done: a memoir on the way, essays on Substack, a growing readership, and original artwork with a cast of characters, including a firefly who turns up throughout her work.

What she didn’t have was a website, and with a book coming, that matters. Agents look authors up, and readers who find an essay want somewhere to go next. A Substack page isn’t a home of your own, and it doesn’t say “this person is serious” the way your own domain does.

The obstacle wasn’t money or time. Domains, hosting and design weren’t her world. Template builders meant doing it herself, and agencies meant proposals and company-sized prices. She wanted one person who would listen to what she had in mind and then make it real.

How the project ran

  1. Understand

    One conversation about what she wanted the site to feel like, who it was for, and what she already had.

  2. Build

    Jason designed the site around her artwork and characters, registered liliturodac.com and connected her Substack sign-up.

  3. Launch

    The site went live two to three weeks after the first call, with a couple of short meetings and some emails on her side.

  4. Support

    She updates her own content in an easy editor. For bigger changes to the site, she emails Jason.

What Pluvium Labs built: a custom author website, integrated with Substack

The project started with a conversation, not a questionnaire. She already had the artwork, the characters and a clear sense of style, so the site didn’t need to invent a brand. It needed to get out of the way of one that already existed.

Designed around the art, not a template

The colors, mood and layout came from her existing work, all under her pen name, with her art in place of a headshot. Characters readers know, like Lux and Lil Nugget, got a place on the site.

The firefly

Her firefly character became the centerpiece of the homepage. It drifts across the page, and clicking it reveals a line from her writing. It’s the site’s signature detail.

Domain and setup

Jason registered liliturodac.com and connected it, so her name is the address. She didn’t have to learn what DNS is.

Integrated with Substack

Her essays stay on Substack, where her readers already are. Her free Substack sign-up appears right on the site, so a new reader can subscribe without leaving.

She updates it herself

An easy content editor lets her add and change her own content whenever she wants, no code and no waiting. For bigger changes to the site itself, she emails Jason, who hosts and supports it.

On a phone: The Tea, with Lux, and the About page, “Meet Lilly,” with her firefly.

The results: live in two to three weeks, ready before the book

The site launched on schedule. For agents, there’s now a professional address to send: her own domain and design, with her essays and art in one place. Most of all, it feels like hers. See it live at liliturodac.com.

What the author says

Common questions

I know nothing about websites. Is that a problem?

No. That was Lilitu Rodac's starting point too. You bring what you want the site to feel like and whatever you already have, like writing, art or a newsletter. Jason handles the domain, design, build and hosting, and explains only as much as you want to know.

Can I update my author website myself?

Yes. Lilitu Rodac updates her own content in an easy editor, with no code, so changes show up on her site right away. For bigger changes to the site itself, she emails Jason.

Do I need a website if I already have Substack?

Substack is a good place to publish, but it isn't a home you own, and agents and readers expect to find one. Lilitu Rodac kept Substack for her essays and added a website around it, integrated with her Substack sign-up.

Should I build an author website before my book comes out?

Yes, ideally. Lilitu Rodac had a memoir on the way and wanted her site live first, so agents and early readers would find a professional home when they looked her up, not just a newsletter.

Can I use a pen name and keep my real name private?

Yes. Lilitu Rodac's site runs entirely under her pen name, and Jason set it up to keep her identity confidential. The domain is registered with privacy protection, so her real name and address don't show up in public domain records. The site, footer, contact email and social links all use the pen name, her art stands in for a headshot, and images are saved without hidden file details.
